# Google: Voltage Fluctuations in Building

## Question 1

**How much can the voltage delivered by an electric utility to a building vary over time?**

The steady-state voltage delivered by an electric utility to a building typically varies within **plus or minus 5% to 6%** of the nominal voltage under normal operating conditions. [[1](https://www.hydroone.com/business-services/commercial-industrial-generators-and-ldcs/power-quality/power-quality-definitions), [2](https://ustpower.com/comparing-automatic-voltage-regulation-technologies/need/avr-guide-utility-voltage-levels/)]

### Normal Voltage Variations

- **Standard Range (Range A):** North American standards (like [ANSI C84.1](https://blog.ansi.org/ansi/ansi-c84-1-2020-electric-voltage-ratings-60-hz/)) and Canadian utility guidelines specify that normal operating voltage at the service entrance should remain within **± 5%** of nominal values (e.g., 114V to 126V for a nominal 120V supply). [[1](https://voltage-disturbance.com/voltage-quality/voltage-tolerance-standard-ansi-c84-1/), [2](https://www.quora.com/What-is-the-percentage-voltage-variation-allowed-at-residential-level-in-the-US), [3](https://www.torontohydro.com/documents/20143/85785/conditions-of-service.pdf/dd339e19-a626-794f-99e2-6daf14e3494c?t=1554732806706)]
- **Daily Fluctuations:** Voltage naturally shifts throughout the day based on local grid demand—it is usually highest at night or on weekends when demand is low, and lowest during late afternoon peak load hours. [, [2](https://ustpower.com/comparing-automatic-voltage-regulation-technologies/need/avr-guide-utility-voltage-levels/)]

### Extended or Extreme Variations

- **Allowable Emergency Range (Range B):** For infrequent, short-term operational events, standards permit wider steady-state deviations, dropping as low as **-8.3% to -13.3%** or rising up to **+5.8%** depending on whether it is measured at the meter or the end-use equipment. [[1](https://www.quora.com/What-is-the-percentage-voltage-variation-allowed-at-residential-level-in-the-US)]
- **Momentary Transients:** Sudden short-duration events like large motor startups, grid faults, lightning strikes, or utility capacitor bank switching can cause brief sags or swells well outside normal tolerances before regulating equipment responds. [[1](https://industrialmonitordirect.com/blogs/knowledgebase/load-flow-study-voltage-levels-ansi-c841-and-ieee-standards), [2](https://www.hydroone.com/business-services/commercial-industrial-generators-and-ldcs/power-quality/power-quality-definitions)]

If you are troubleshooting a specific issue, tell me:

- What is the **nominal voltage** (e.g., 120V, 240V, 600V)?
- Are you seeing **sags (low voltage)** or **swells (high voltage)**?



## Question 2

**Nominal voltage is 600V, I'm interested in the fluctuations in the voltage delivered by a step-down transformer that takes 600V to 208V.**

The steady-state voltage delivered by a 600V-to-208V step-down transformer typically varies between **197.6V and 218.4V** under normal operating conditions.

Because transformers inherently pass through and proportionally scale the utility grid's voltage fluctuations, any changes on the 600V primary side directly impact the 208V secondary side.

### Standard Operating Ranges

According to industry standards like CSA C235 in Canada and [ANSI C84.1](https://blog.ansi.org/) in the US, voltage variations are classified into distinct service ranges:

- **Normal Range (Range A):** This represents standard daily operations. The voltage stays within **± 5%** of nominal values.
  - Primary (600V nominal): **570V to 630V**
  - Secondary (208V nominal): **197.6V to 218.4V**
- **Extreme Range (Range B):** This accounts for infrequent peak load conditions or unusual grid stress. The voltage is legally allowed to drop down to **-8.3%** or rise up to **+5.8%** for short periods.
  - Primary (600V nominal): **550V to 635V**
  - Secondary (208V nominal): **190.7V to 220V**

### Factors Influencing the Variations

- **Transformer Impedance Drops:** As current load increases inside the building, internal resistance within the transformer causes an internal voltage drop (usually an extra 2% to 5% loss at full load).
- **Primary Grid Fluctuations:** If the utility's 600V supply drops due to regional peak demands, the 208V output drops proportionally based on the transformer's fixed turn ratio.
- **Transformer Tap Settings:** Most commercial step-down transformers feature manual de-energized tap changers (typically providing adjustments in steps of **±2.5%**). If your local utility consistently delivers a voltage that is too high or too low, these physical taps are adjusted to shift the entire baseline up or down.
